content.prompt: Which line of Python safely queries the database using the variable name?
options: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'")
cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s" % name)
content.why: A parameterised query sends the value separately from the SQL, so input can't change the query. The other three build the SQL string from user input.

content.prompt: Which measures reduce the risk or impact of cross-site scripting (XSS)? Select ALL that apply.

content.prompt: Distinguish between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.
criteria: Clearly distinguishes between the two, with reference to keys
content.sample: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key to both encrypt and decrypt, which is fast but means the key has to be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key, so no secret has to be shared, but it is much slower. HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption to agree on a symmetric session key.

content.prompt:
A login function is shown.
def login(username, password):
    query = ("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + username +
             "' AND password = '" + password + "'")
    return db.execute(query).fetchone()

(a) Explain how entering admin' -- as the username could let an attacker log in without the password. (2 marks)

(b) Rewrite the function so it is secure. Assume each user's password is stored as a bcrypt hash in a column called password_hash. (2 marks)
criteria: (a) Explains that the input closes the string and that -- comments out the password check, so the query matches the admin row
(b) Uses a parameterised query AND checks the password against the stored hash
content.sample:
(a) The query becomes ... WHERE username = 'admin' --' AND password = '...'. The quote ends the username string, and -- turns the rest of the line into a comment, so the password condition is never checked. The query returns the admin row and the attacker is logged in. This is SQL injection.

import bcrypt

def login(username, password):
    row = db.execute(
        "SELECT password_hash FROM users WHERE username = ?",
        (username,)).fetchone()
    return row is not None and bcrypt.checkpw(password.encode(), row[0])

content.prompt: A school is building an app that stores students' names, contact details and timetables. Describe how the principles of privacy by design could be applied to this app.
criteria: Describes several privacy by design principles, each applied to the app
Outlines some principles with some link to the app
content.sample: Privacy is built in from the start rather than added after a breach. The app should collect only the data it needs (data minimisation): for example, no home address if timetables don't need it. Privacy should be the default, so contact details are hidden from other students unless a student chooses to share them. Data should be protected end to end: encrypted in transit with HTTPS and at rest in the database, with access limited by role. The school should be transparent through a clear privacy policy, and data should be deleted when a student leaves.

content.prompt:
A web app keeps users logged in using a session cookie.

(a) Outline how a session cookie keeps a user logged in between page requests. (2 marks)

(b) Describe TWO ways to make the session more secure. (2 marks)
criteria: (a) Outlines that the server creates a session ID after login, the browser stores it in a cookie and sends it with each request, and the server looks it up
content.sample:
(a) After a successful login the server creates a random session ID, stores it with the user's details, and sends it to the browser in a cookie. HTTP is stateless, so the browser sends the cookie with every later request, and the server looks up the ID to know who the user is.

(b) Any two: set the Secure flag so the cookie is only sent over HTTPS; set HttpOnly so JavaScript (and so an XSS attack) can't read it; set SameSite to reduce CSRF; make sessions expire after inactivity and on logout; regenerate the session ID after login to prevent session fixation.

content.prompt:
A database has these tables:

Students(id, name, year)
Results(student_id, subject, mark)

Write an SQL query that lists the name and mark of every Year 12 student who scored 80 or more in Software Engineering, highest mark first.
criteria: Correct query with join, all three conditions and correct ordering
content.sample:
SELECT Students.name, Results.mark
FROM Students
JOIN Results ON Students.id = Results.student_id
WHERE Students.year = 12
  AND Results.subject = 'Software Engineering'
  AND Results.mark >= 80
ORDER BY Results.mark DESC;

content.prompt: Outline TWO ways that following the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) improves a website for its users.
content.sample: Any two: alt text on images lets screen readers describe them to vision-impaired users; sufficient colour contrast makes text readable for people with low vision or colour blindness; full keyboard navigation helps people who can't use a mouse; captions help deaf or hard-of-hearing users; clear headings and labels make the page easier for everyone to follow.

content.prompt:
Write a Python function validate_password(pw) that returns a list of the rules the password fails, in this order:
  • "length" if it has fewer than 12 characters
  • "digit" if it has no digit
  • "uppercase" if it has no uppercase letter
  • "symbol" if it has none of the characters !@#$%^&*
A password that passes every rule returns an empty list. For example, validate_password("longpassword12") returns ["uppercase", "symbol"].
criteria: Correct function that passes all tests, including an empty list for a valid password
Correct function with one minor error
content.sample:
def validate_password(pw):
    failed = []
    if len(pw) < 12:
        failed.append("length")
    if not any(c.isdigit() for c in pw):
        failed.append("digit")
    if not any(c.isupper() for c in pw):
        failed.append("uppercase")
    if not any(c in "!@#$%^&*" for c in pw):
        failed.append("symbol")
    return failed

Tests: "Short1!" gives ["length"]; "longpassword12" gives ["uppercase", "symbol"]; "Correct#Horse9Battery" gives [].

content.prompt: Explain what overfitting is, and ONE way to prevent it.
criteria: Explains overfitting and a valid way to prevent it
Outlines overfitting or a prevention method
content.sample: Overfitting is when a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, so it scores well on training data but poorly on new data. It can be prevented by testing on a separate validation set and stopping training when validation error starts rising (early stopping), or by using more training data or a simpler model.

content.prompt:
A model predicts a student's test score ŷ from the hours studied x using the regression line ŷ = 6x + 40.

(a) Predict the score of a student who studies for 7 hours. (1 mark)

(b) Explain why the model is unreliable for a student who studies for 20 hours. (2 marks)

(c) The model is tested on three students: (2 hours, 50), (5 hours, 72) and (8 hours, 86). Calculate the mean squared error. (1 mark)
criteria: (b) Explains that 20 hours is outside the range of the training data (extrapolation) and the prediction of 160 exceeds the maximum possible score
content.sample:
(a) 6 × 7 + 40 = 82

(b) The model predicts 6 × 20 + 40 = 160, which is impossible on a test out of 100. Twenty hours is outside the range of the data the model was trained on, so this is extrapolation: the straight-line relationship probably doesn't hold (returns diminish as scores approach the maximum).

(c) Predictions are 52, 70 and 88. Errors are −2, 2 and −2, so squared errors are 4, 4 and 4. MSE = (4 + 4 + 4) ÷ 3 = 4.

content.prompt: Evaluate the impact of automation through machine learning on employment and on society.
criteria: Makes a well-supported judgement, with detailed positive and negative effects on both employment and society and relevant examples
Describes positive and negative effects on employment and society
content.sample:
Employment: ML automates repetitive, rules-based tasks such as data entry, invoice processing and basic customer service, which reduces those jobs and puts most pressure on low-skilled workers. At the same time it creates new roles (data scientists, ML engineers, people who maintain and audit models) and frees workers from dangerous or tedious work. The net effect depends on reskilling: workers whose jobs change need training to move into the new roles.

Society: automation lowers costs and enables new services, such as faster medical image screening and fraud detection. However, models trained on biased data can make unfair decisions in hiring, lending or policing at a large scale, and "black box" models make those decisions hard to explain or challenge. Large datasets also raise privacy concerns, and the benefits can flow mainly to the companies that own the technology, widening inequality.

Judgement: overall the impact is positive for productivity and safety, but only if it is managed: governments and businesses need to invest in reskilling and require transparency and bias testing in high-stakes decisions.

content.prompt:
A single neuron has inputs x₁ = 2 and x₂ = 3, weights w₁ = 0.5 and w₂ = −1, a bias of 1 and a ReLU activation function, where ReLU(z) = max(0, z).

(a) Calculate the neuron's output. Show your working. (2 marks)

(b) Outline how training would change this neuron if its output was too low. (2 marks)
criteria: (a) Correct weighted sum or a correct method
(b) Outlines that the error is backpropagated and the weights and bias are adjusted (gradient descent) to reduce the error
content.sample:
(a) z = (0.5 × 2) + (−1 × 3) + 1 = 1 − 3 + 1 = −1. Output = ReLU(−1) = max(0, −1) = 0.

(b) A loss function measures how far the output is from the target. Backpropagation calculates how much each weight and the bias contributed to that error, and gradient descent adjusts them by a small amount (set by the learning rate), for example increasing w₂ or the bias so z becomes positive. This repeats over many examples until the error is low.

content.prompt:
A library system stores items. Every LibraryItem has a title and an item_id, and a method describe() that returns a string. A Book is a LibraryItem that also has an author. A DVD is a LibraryItem that also has a runtime in minutes. Book and DVD each override describe() to include their extra attribute.

Write Python code for all three classes.
criteria: All three classes correct: subclasses extend LibraryItem, call super().__init__, add their attribute and override describe()
Mostly correct with one error (for example a missing super().__init__)
Superclass and at least one subclass mostly correct
content.sample:
class LibraryItem:
    def __init__(self, title, item_id):
        self.title = title
        self.item_id = item_id

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.item_id}: {self.title}"


class Book(LibraryItem):
    def __init__(self, title, item_id, author):
        super().__init__(title, item_id)
        self.author = author

    def describe(self):
        return f"{super().describe()} by {self.author}"


class DVD(LibraryItem):
    def __init__(self, title, item_id, runtime):
        super().__init__(title, item_id)
        self.runtime = runtime

    def describe(self):
        return f"{super().describe()} ({self.runtime} min)"

content.prompt: With reference to your code in the previous question, explain how it shows generalisation, inheritance and polymorphism. Use the terms superclass and subclass.
criteria: Explains all three concepts with correct terms and specific reference to the code
Explains two, or all three with limited reference to the code
content.sample: Generalisation: the attributes and behaviour common to every item (title, item_id, describe()) are moved up into the superclass LibraryItem instead of being repeated. Inheritance: Book and DVD are subclasses that inherit title, item_id and describe() from LibraryItem, and call super().__init__() so the superclass sets them up. Polymorphism: each subclass overrides describe(), so calling item.describe() on a list of mixed Books and DVDs runs the right version for each object without the caller checking its type.

content.prompt:
A team is building a canteen ordering app using Scrum.

(a) Write a user story for ordering lunch, with TWO acceptance criteria. (2 marks)

(b) Explain how working in sprints helps the team manage changing requirements. (2 marks)
criteria: (a) User story in the correct form with two testable acceptance criteria
(b) Explains how short iterations with feedback and a reprioritised backlog absorb change
content.sample:
(a) As a student, I want to order and pay for my lunch before recess so that I don't have to queue. Acceptance criteria: orders close at 10:30 am on the day; the student receives an order number and an order summary on screen after paying.

(b) Each sprint is a short, fixed period (usually 1 to 4 weeks) that ends with working software shown to the client in a sprint review. Feedback and new requirements are added to the product backlog and reprioritised before the next sprint starts, so changes are absorbed every few weeks instead of forcing a redesign of a plan fixed at the start.

content.prompt: A school canteen app lets students log in, order food and pay online. Justify FOUR security measures the developers should build into the app, covering different parts of the system.
criteria: Justifies four appropriate measures across different parts of the system, each linked to a specific threat
Describes three or four measures with some justification
content.sample: Authentication: store passwords as salted hashes (bcrypt) and offer multi-factor authentication, so a stolen database doesn't reveal passwords and a guessed password alone can't take over an account. Input handling: validate all input on the server and use parameterised queries and output encoding, which stops SQL injection and XSS through order notes or names. Network: serve everything over HTTPS with Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite cookies, so payment and login data can't be read or changed in transit and sessions can't be stolen. Payments and data: use a certified payment provider instead of storing card details, and give the database account least privilege. Testing and monitoring: run SAST and DAST before release and log logins and orders, so vulnerabilities are found early and suspicious activity can be traced (accountability).
